Rust for Project Intent: How AFWE Caught Its Own Architectural Blindspots

Rust made memory mistakes impossible to make quietly. AFWE makes regressions of intent impossible to make quietly. Inside the dogfooding post-mortem that proved how silent capability severance happens—and the deterministic ratchets that stop it.

AFWE Core Architecture Team • October 27, 2026 • 10 min read

"Rust for project intent." Rust made memory mistakes impossible to make quietly. AFWE makes regressions of intent impossible to make quietly. "Quietly" is the word that keeps the claim honest: you can still break things on purpose, but you can never break them by accident.

Last week, AFWE had an uncomfortable moment. During our own dogfooding iterations on branch ReBorn, an autonomous agent retired legacy v1 workflows in Turn t0022. In doing so, it removed the caller to contract::task_start in the CLI crate, but crates/afwe-core/src/contract.rs was never touched.

The function went completely dead. At the exact same time, duplicate briefing logic was written into turn.begin instead of reusing context::scope_matches. AFWE's commit gate committed cleanly. The tool built to stop silent architectural decay had failed to catch dead code and duplication in its own engine.

Rather than paper over the failure with prompt engineering, we stopped development and initiated an exhaustive post-mortem. This article documents what broke, the fierce debates and pushbacks during design, and the multi-level deterministic ratchets that now guarantee this failure mode is physically impossible.

1. The Blindspot: Why Checking Touched Files Misses the Real World

Most static analysis and code verification systems operate under a flawed assumption: inspect only the files changed in the pull request.

In our Turn t0022 incident, the agent edited crates/afwe-cli/src/main.rs. It deleted the call site of contract::task_start. Because crates/afwe-core/src/contract.rs had 0 git diff bytes, the commit gate never analyzed contract.rs.

Turn t0022 git diff:
  M crates/afwe-cli/src/main.rs         [-contract::task_start(...)]
  [crates/afwe-core/src/contract.rs]   [UNTOUCHED — 0 bytes diff]
Gate verdict: PASSED (Blindspot: callee was severed in an untouched file)

A function almost never goes dead because someone deleted the function itself; it goes dead because someone removed its caller, which sits in a completely different file. Checking only touched files makes cross-module severance completely invisible.

2. The Design Debate: Concessions, Pushbacks, and Realities

When fixing this blindspot, we initially proposed tracking dead code down to every struct field, enum variant, and cross-file import edge. That proposal triggered severe pushback from our core architects:

  • The "0% False Positives" Overclaim: Pure import-edge diffing fails on dynamic dispatch (engine.run()), trait objects, glob imports (use contract::*), and macro registrations. A tree-sitter AST parser cannot statically prove which run() was invoked without full compiler type resolution. The resolution: We over-approximate edges. Any identifier occurrence anywhere in code counts as an inbound reference. Errors only ever go in the safe direction: we may miss an unused function with a generic name, but we will never falsely block live code.
  • Conceding Struct Fields & Enum Variants to the Compiler: Struct fields and enum variants are deeply affected by serialization frameworks (Serde, Jackson, Pydantic). A struct field might only ever be populated via JSON deserialization and never constructed directly in code. Attempting to track fields statically produces intolerable false alarms. Furthermore, rustc -D dead_code already catches private unused items. We conceded this domain to the compiler.
  • Grandfathering Pre-Existing Debt: If you run a dead-code gate on an established repository, it will flag hundreds of existing legacy functions on Day 1. Developers experience alert fatigue and disable the tool. The resolution: AFWE ratchets against a baseline. Pre-existing zero-reference symbols are grandfathered in baseline.yaml. The gate strictly blocks newly severed capabilities (>0 → 0) and functions born dead in touched files.
  • Tamper-Resistant Root Inference: If an agent can arbitrarily add dead functions to an "exempt roots" list in the manifest to silence the gate, the ratchet is gamed. We enforce automatic root inference (main.rs, lib.rs, index.ts, tests/**) and treat manual root edits like pin modifications—requiring an explicit override reason.

3. The Final Solution: A Two-Prong Architecture

The resulting implementation divides architectural governance into two high-leverage engines:

Prong 1: Decision-to-Code Link Ratchet (AFWE's Unique Superpower)

Existing linters only analyze code syntax; they know nothing of human architectural intent. In AFWE, active architectural decisions (.afwe/memory/**/*.md), pinned invariants (.afwe/pins/*.yaml), and documentation link directly to blueprint nodes, files, and symbols.

  • ORPHANED_DECISION: Blocks if a symbol, file, or node anchored to an active decision vanishes without an explicit supersede or update.
  • ORPHANED_PIN: Blocks if a pinned invariant loses its implementing code.
  • DOCS_DRIFT: Blocks if markdown documentation links point to deleted code files.

Prong 2: Minimal Cross-Boundary Inbound-Reference Ratchet

A single-pass ASCII identifier scanner tokenizes all project files in under 15 milliseconds. It compares workspace-wide reference counts between turn begin and turn commit.

  • SEVERED_CAPABILITY: Flags when an exported symbol drops from >0 to 0 inbound references, catching cross-module caller deletions even if the callee file was never modified!
  • DEAD_ON_ARRIVAL: Flags newly introduced exported symbols born with 0 references in touched files, forcing agents to either wire them up, test them in tests/, or declare them in turn intents.
IMPORTANT: Over-Approximation Policy & Guarantees

Over-Approximation Policy (Safe Error Direction): To prevent false alarms on dynamic dispatch, macros, or string lookups, the identifier index over-approximates references. Any identifier token occurrence in code counts as a reference.

  • The Guarantee: AFWE will never falsely block live code.
  • The Trade-off: Generic names (new, len, init, run, default, get, set) are intentionally treated as always referenced and unflaggable.
  • Language-Adaptive: Weakly typed languages (Python/JS) leverage identifier token matching across files; typed languages (Rust/Go/TS) leverage module-scoped import specifiers where available.

4. Proving the Fix: The Interactive Demo

To test these capabilities in your own terminal, we updated the official AFWE test harness with dedicated cross-module capability tests. You can run the interactive walkthrough in bash or PowerShell: 

# On Linux / macOS
./scripts/demo.sh

# On Windows (PowerShell)
.scriptsdemo.ps1

During Step 3 of the demo, the script simulates the exact t0022 bug: it modifies checkout.ts and removes the call to charge2, leaving charge.ts untouched. Watch the commit gate intercept the regression:

> afwe turn commit t0003
• REDO — t0003 NOT committed
  ✖ SEVERED_CAPABILITY: 'src/payments/charge.ts::charge2' lost all incoming callers (dropped from 1 to 0) — restore caller, wire it in, or declare it in turn assume with action remove or replace
→ fix the failures above, then call turn.commit again. Nothing was committed.

The gate refuses to commit until the engineer or agent explicitly declares the intent: 

# In assume.json:
{
  "intents": [
    { "id": "decouple-charge", "action": "update", "targets": ["payments"] },
    { "id": "deprecate-charge2", "action": "replace", "targets": ["src/payments/charge.ts"] }
  ]
}

5. Conclusion: What "Quietly" Really Means

Rust does not prevent you from using unsafe to dereference a raw pointer when you genuinely need to write low-level hardware drivers. What Rust guarantees is that you cannot dereference a null pointer quietly. The compiler forces you to write unsafe { ... }, recording the trade-off explicitly in source code.

AFWE does the same for architectural intent. If you want to retire a capability, delete a module, or break an architectural boundary, AFWE does not stop you. But you cannot do it quietly. You cannot do it because an LLM hallucinated, lost context, or forgot what was agreed upon three turns ago. You must declare the intent in turn assume, record the rationale, and sign the commit.

You can break things on purpose. You can never break them by accident.
